sum: Trillions of dollars has been wiped off the stock value of major tech firms in the US, Europe and Asia in a market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) development.
Shares in firms across the tech sector plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5% on Thursday, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide.
The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6.3% lower in the afternoon as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost almost 11.5% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 5.8%.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 8.8%, while Samsung was down by around 6%.

sum: NEW YORK — U.S. stocks are mixed, as AI chip companies fall again while AppLovin and Tapestry rally after reporting stronger profits than analysts expected. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent Thursday, coming off its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 265 points, and the Nasdaq composite fell 1.1 per cent. AI-related stocks worldwide felt pressure from worries that Tuesday’s U.S. elections could mean moratoriums for data centers in some areas, and South Korea’s Kopi index tumbled 5.3 per cent. In other markets, though, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the midterms faded. Oil prices recovered some of their sharp slides, while Treasury yields steadied.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
World shares were mostly higher Thursday, though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections.

South Korea’s Kospi sank more than five per cent and the Nikkei 225 in Tokyo lost nearly two per cent. Oil prices were mixed after the Dow industrials jumped more than three per cent on Wednesday following the Republicans’ loss of control of the U.S. Congress.
In early European trading, the German DAX rose 0.6 per cent to 26,598.03, while the CAC 40 in Paris surged 1.2 per cent to 8,276.55. The United Kingdom’s FTSE 100 gained 1 per cent to 10,935.08.

The future for the S&P 500 was nearly unchanged, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.4 per cent. On Wednesday, the S&P 500 jumped 1.6 per cent. The Dow surged more than 1,500 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4 per cent.

U.S. stocks usually climb following midterms, regardless of who wins. But technology shares have taken a hit as investors mull the potential impact on the boom in AI from a Congress led by Democratic Party lawmakers from January.

sum: US stocks crash: US stock markets has witnessed a sharp selloff on Friday, with the Nasdaq Composite falling nearly 3 per cent as disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon reignited concerns over heavy investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and the time companies may take to generate returns.

All three major US stock indexes ended the session in the red, with technology stocks bearing the brunt of the selling pressure. The Nasdaq recorded its biggest single-day percentage decline since June 5, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq also ended October with monthly losses, Reuters reported.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 571.98 points, or 1.09 , to close at 51,770.58. The S&P 500 dropped 139.30 points, or 1.80 per cent, to settle at 7,580.21, while the Nasdaq Composite plunged 747.73 points, or 2.84 per cent, to 25,440.68.
In terms of market capitalisation, the Dow Jones lost USD 312.22 billion, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite shed USD 1.23 trillion and USD 1.20 trillion, respectively.

The latest selloff followed quarterly results from Intel and Amazon, released late Thursday, which failed to meet investor expectations. The results brought renewed attention to the rising cost of building AI infrastructure and questions over whether companies will be able to generate adequate returns from their investments.
Chip stocks faced heavy selling pressure, dragging the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index towards a monthly loss.
Investors are increasingly scrutinising the scale of AI spending and the timeline for companies to turn these investments into profits.

sum: US stocks ended October 30, 2026, with their sharpest technology-led selloff in months, as disappointing corporate earnings and mounting concerns about artificial intelligence investment costs prompted investors to reassess Wall Street valuations.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.86% to 25,437, its worst daily performance since June. The S&P 500 declined 1.82% to 7,580, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 572.25 points, or 1.09%, closing at 51,770.31.

Despite the selloff, major investment banks remain divided over the outlook for US equities. Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and J.P. Morgan maintain year-end S&P 500 targets of 8,000, while Citigroup and UBS project 8,100. Bank of America takes a more cautious position, forecasting 7,400.
- US stocks fell sharply on October 30, with the Nasdaq losing 2.86%, S&P 500 declining 1.82% and Dow Jones dropping 1.09% amid concerns over AI spending.
- Wall Street’s 2026 S&P 500 forecasts range from 7,400 at Bank of America to 8,100 at Citi and UBS. Morgan Stanley warns of possible short-term downside to 7,100–7,200.
- S&P 500 Q3 earnings rose an estimated 30.2%, with 82% of companies beating expectations. However, elevated valuations, margin debt and AI financing costs threaten further volatility.

sum: Intel logged a lower profit in the third quarter and guided for lackluster fourth-quarter earnings, sending shares sliding after-hours.

The chip maker on Thursday projected that adjusted earnings in the current fourth quarter of 25 cents a share, on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet were expecting fourth-quarter earnings of 45 cents a share on $17.29 billion of revenue.
Shares fell 17% to $76.85 in after-hours trading. The stock closed down 3.6% at $92.07, and has more than doubled in price this year through the close.
The company reported a third-quarter profit of $3.32 billion, or 60 cents a share. That compares with a profit of $4.06 billion, or 90 cents a share, a year earlier.
Stripping out certain one-time items, adjusted earnings were 52 cents a share. Analysts polled by FactSet were expecting 41 cents a share.
Revenue grew 21% to $16.51 billion, missing analyst expectations for $16.56 billion.
While revenue from the company's data center and AI segment surged 78% to $7.3 billion, the client computing and physical AI group had revenue decline 5% to $8.1 billion.

Geopolitically, the Trump administration drafted a post-war Middle East strategy targeting Iran and regional normalization, while escalating pressure on the central bank for monetary easing.

TradingKey - Affected by stronger-than-expected US August non-farm payrolls data, major US stock indices fell as market expectations grew that the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates at its next policy meeting. Tesla held the Cybercab event in Austin, Texas on Thursday, which was invite-only, not livestreamed, and not attended by CEO Elon Musk. The company stated that users can experience the Cybercab driverless service within a limited area in Austin via the Tesla Robotaxi ride-hailing app. An analyst at RBC Capital Markets noted that Tesla disclosed limited new information at the event, leaving key issues such as pricing, production cadence, and regulatory approvals unresolved.

However, Trump's warning to raise tariffs on Canadian automobiles to 50% dampened market sentiment. The yield on a Broadcom bond with a 5.15% coupon maturing in 2031 has risen by about 14 basis points since August, signaling pressure on bond prices. Meanwhile, the company's 5-year credit default swap (CDS) spread widened by about 28 basis points over the same period, surpassing increases for Oracle and SpaceX. Broadcom is currently negotiating a debt financing deal exceeding $60 billion with financial institutions to help AI companies, including Anthropic, purchase chips and related infrastructure. While the transaction structure remains under discussion, Broadcom may provide credit support for a portion of the senior secured debt.

sum: US stocks stayed flat as Iran tensions pushed oil above $80, while Intel fell and investors weighed Fed rate bets, inflation data and key stock moves.

US stocks opened mostly flat on Monday as investors remained worried about whether the US and Iran can reach a lasting deal over the Strait of Hormuz. The uncertainty kept investors cautious at the start of the week.

The S&P 500 was up about 0.1%, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 110 points, or 0.2%, during the session. The three major US stock indexes were coming off their best weekly performance since April. The S&P 500 also ended last week at a record closing high.
The biggest issue for markets on Monday was the uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil shipments.
Iran has said it is getting closer to a deal with Oman that could allow more ships to move through the Strait of Hormuz. However, Tehran has not agreed to restart direct talks with Washington.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that there was no possibility of restarting negotiations while the US continued to violate a June memorandum of understanding and had not compensated Iran for those violations. Tasnim News Agency, a semi-official Iranian outlet linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, reported his comments.
The mixed signals from the US and Iran made investors less confident that a deal to reopen the important shipping route would happen soon.

sum: U.S. stocks fell sharply in midday trading Wednesday as geopolitical tensions reignited and investors positioned ahead of the Federal Reserve's 2:00 p.m. ET policy decision. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -0.02%) is down 1.7% at mid-day, led lower by Caterpillar (CAT +0.81%) dropping 7.3% and Goldman Sachs (GS +1.30%) falling 4.6% on macroeconomic concerns. The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.68%) has shed 1%, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.12%) is down by 1.3%.
All three indexes opened in the red, made a half-hearted attempt at stabilization around 11 a.m. ET, then gave up and slid lower again.
The immediate trigger for today's selling? Oil prices rocketing more than 6%.

President Donald Trump told Fox News the U.S. would give Iran "a beating" following an overnight missile attack on American forces. That was the end of last Friday's diplomatic progress. You know the ripple effects that follow when oil prices are on the move. Every company depends on energy in some way, so high oil prices quickly get expensive for retailers, tech giants, and manufacturers.

Then there's the Fed. At 2:00 p.m., Chairman Kevin Warsh will announce the latest policy decision, and futures markets are pricing in a nearly 70% chance that rates stay put in the current 3.5% to 3.75% range. But the real drama will come during Warsh's press conference, where traders will parse every word for hints on whether the Fed is sticking with "higher-for-longer" or if recent oil price swings and stubborn inflation readings are raising fresh concerns.

Semiconductor stocks bore the brunt of the technology sector sell-off. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX +2.07%) plunged 4.4%, extending a 10% weekly decline. Micron Technology (MU +5.46%) dropped 5.7%, and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +8.29%) fell 5.8%. They didn't do anything wrong, other than being richly valued growth stocks on a de-risking kind of market day.
And it's earnings season. Sherwin-Williams (SHW -1.62%) beat analyst estimates and Boeing (BA -0.11%) posted a mixed report. Both stocks fell, erasing a combined 109 points from the Dow.

Stock markets: Seoul sends fresh shockwaves through the tech sector; Wall Street sees volatility, Milan down 0.7%
sum: Following the turbulence in the early part of the session, Wall Street is attempting to shake off concerns about AI by focusing on quarterly results. Oil prices are still falling, down by more than 5 per cent. Saipem shares plummet on the Milan Stock Exchange

(Il Sole 24 Ore Radiocor) – A new shockwave from Asia is hitting the tech sector, spreading to Europe, with share prices holding steady except for the FTSE MIB in Milan (FTSE MIB), dragged down by Stmicroelectronics and Prysmian as well as by Saipem . The sell-off hit the Tokyo Stock Exchange (Nikkei 225 ) and the Seoul Stock Exchange (-10.8%), partly due to rumours of significant advances by China in semiconductor technology. The announcement was interpreted as a sign of China’s ability to narrow the gap with Western technologies in a sector considered crucial for artificial intelligence. Consequently, Samsung Electronics (-13%) and SK hynix (-13.7%) – which together account for around half of the Kospi’s market capitalisation – took a hit, making the index more susceptible to fluctuations linked to market sentiment regarding the technology sector.

But the downturn in the tech sector has not spared Wall Street either, where tech shares have entered a correction phase, following the collapse of global chip manufacturers, whilst fears are mounting over the resilience of the AI sector ahead of the US Big Tech firms’ earnings reports. As a result, the Nasdaq 100 index has lost over 10 per cent from its all-time high in early June. In the background, attention remains focused, on the one hand, on the Fed’s interest rate decision due on Wednesday, and on the other, developments in the Middle East, with talks between the US and Iran appearing to proceed despite mutual threats. However, the market appears to believe that an agreement is possible, and the price of oil continues to fall.

Wall Street closes on a mixed note. The Dow Jones rose by 1.03% to 52,747.53 points, the Nasdaq fell by 0.22% to 24,876.91 points, whilst the S&P 500 rose by 0.22% to 7,429.22 points, buoyed, like the Dow Jones, by quarterly results and the fall in oil prices.

sum: Never miss an important update on your stock portfolio and cut through the noise. Over 7 million investors trust Simply Wall St to stay informed where it matters for FREE.
- If you are wondering whether Dow is priced attractively or not, the stock's recent moves and valuation checks offer plenty to think about.
- Dow closed at US$27.92, with the share price up 15.0% year to date and 11.0% over the past year, even though it declined 9.3% in the last week and fell 17.3% over the past month.

- Those short term declines sit against a longer track record where the stock fell 38.2% over three years and declined 42.3% over five years. This mixed history can shape how investors view both the current risks and any potential recovery story behind Dow.

- On Simply Wall St's valuation checklist, Dow scores a full 6 out of 6 for being assessed as undervalued. This sets up a closer look at how different valuation methods stack up and hints at an even more useful way to think about fair value later in the article.

A Discounted Cash Flow model estimates what a stock might be worth by taking projected future cash flows, then discounting them back to today to reflect risk and the time value of money. For Dow, this DCF uses a 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to Equity approach, based on cash flow projections expressed in $.

Dow's latest twelve month free cash flow shows an outflow of $591.1m, so the model leans heavily on expectations that cash flows turn positive and stabilize over time. Analyst inputs cover the earlier years, while Simply Wall St extrapolates the later years. By 2028, free cash flow is projected at $2.0b, with a full set of ten year projections ranging between about $1.7b and $2.4b across the period.
